did_you_know.text: Did you know? Three central symbols of the devastation appear at the very beginning of the psalm: the Lord’s inheritance, His holy temple, and Jerusalem. The nations are described as invading the inheritance, defiling the temple, and reducing the city to ruins.

Did you know? The dead are described with two terms expressing their belonging to the Lord: “Your servants” and “Your faithful ones.” The verse emphasizes the disgrace inflicted on their bodies by giving them as food to birds and wild animals.

Did you know? The pouring out of blood “like water” is an image of the scale of the slaughter and the abundance of blood. The words “with no one to bury them” add a picture of disaster in which the dead receive no burial.

Did you know? The destruction is presented not only as a national disaster but also as a public humiliation: the people have become “a reproach,” “a taunt,” and “a laughingstock” to their neighbors and those around them.
Did you know? At the center of the psalm appears a direct question to the Lord: “How long?” The psalmist describes God’s anger as a burning fire, expressing a sense of an ongoing crisis.

Did you know? The psalmist asks that God’s anger be directed against the nations “that do not know You” and against the kingdoms that have not called on the Lord’s name. In this way, he connects the enemies’ actions with their attitude toward the Lord’s name.

Did you know? Alongside the request for judgment on the enemies, the people also ask for mercy for themselves: “Do not remember against us the sins of our ancestors.” This request emphasizes the people’s weakness and their need for swift mercy.

Did you know? In this verse, salvation and forgiveness are requested “for the sake of Your name.” In other words, the psalmist presents the people’s rescue as also serving to preserve the honor of the Lord’s name in the eyes of the nations.

Did you know? The psalm explicitly mentions “the groaning of the prisoner” and asks the Lord to hear it. It also says, “According to the greatness of Your power”—an expression of the strength needed to save those destined to die.

Did you know? The ending moves from describing the disaster to making a commitment for the future: the people present themselves as “Your people and the sheep of Your pasture” and promise to give thanks and proclaim the Lord’s praise from generation to generation.
